ann_113.text: Through this part, moving from 7 to 13 on the 1-16 education scale clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 86% to about 32%, being 58 rather than 22 years old clearly lowers it from about 76% to about 41%, and capital losses of $1,887 clearly lower it from about 63% to about 28%.

Compared with a husband married to a civilian spouse, it clearly gives a wife a lower chance (about 19%), and a higher one to someone's own child, another relative or someone listed as unmarried (about 96%), anyone not married to a civilian spouse (about 91%), people not in a family (about 75%) and women (about 84%).

Farming or fishing (about 90%), handlers or cleaners (about 85%), a missing work class (about 79%), machine operators or inspectors (about 78%), self-employment without incorporation (about 77%), the occupations this part does not tell apart (about 73%) and sales (about 68%) clearly raise it, and federal government work (about 48%), executive or managerial jobs (about 54%) and technical support (about 58%) clearly lower it.

Compared with a high-school education, a 5th-6th grade (about 38%), 10th grade (about 56%) or 7th-8th grade education (about 57%) lowers it, and an academic associate degree raises it to about 72% (on the training data only).

On the training data only, being born in Colombia (above 99%), Vietnam (about 86%), China or the Dominican Republic (about 82%), Puerto Rico or Ecuador (about 74%) raises it, being born in the Philippines (about 26%), Yugoslavia (about 27%), Italy (about 45%), England (about 52%), Cuba or Canada (about 56%) lowers it, being Black or American Indian or Eskimo raises it to about 69%, and a higher census sampling weight lowers it from about 65% to about 60%.
Never having worked raises it to above 99% (9 people), and being born in Laos to about 98% (17 people, on the training data only); the model has little data on this.

ann_114.text: Through this part, capital gains of $6,849 rather than none clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 5%.
Work outside the private sector lowers it only slightly through this part (it stays at about 63%), on the training data only.

ann_115.text: Through this part, working 55 rather than 24 hours a week clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 82% to about 46%.
Being born in Thailand (26 people) clearly raises it from about 63% to about 84%.

ann_116.text: Through this part, a preschool education clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to above 99%.
Protective service work lowers it to about 40% (on the training data only).

ann_117.text: Through this part, a bachelor's degree slightly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 63% to about 68% (on the training data only).

ann_118.text: Through this part, other service jobs clearly raise a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 91%.
Being born in Iran raises it to about 88% (on the training data only).
Unpaid work raises it to about 77%, but the model has little data on this (17 people), on the training data only.

ann_119.text: Through this part, being listed in the household as unmarried clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 24% (although the whole model gives these people a higher chance, about 81%).

ann_120.text: Through this part, being born in Honduras lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 3%, but the model has little data on this (14 people), on the training data only.

ann_121.text: Through this part, being never married raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 70% (on the training data only).

ann_122.text: This part acts only on the 652 of 39,073 people in the training data with a professional school degree, and 165 of them had an income of $50,000 or less.
Through it, a professional school degree slightly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 63% to about 59% (on the training data only).

For the typical person it acts on (a 44-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, with a professional school degree and a professional specialty job in the private sector, working 48 hours a week), it slightly lowers the predicted chance from about 9% to about 7% (on the training data only).

ann_123.text: For a typical person, the model clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less with capital gains of $6,849 (about 63% to 5%) or capital losses of $1,887 (to about 28%), as the education scale rises from 7 to 13 (about 86% to 32%), as weekly hours rise from 24 to 55 (about 82% to 46%) and as age rises from 22 to 58 years (about 76% to 41%).

Compared with a husband married to a civilian spouse, it clearly gives a wife a lower chance (about 19%), and a higher one to someone's own child or another relative (about 96%), never-married people (about 93%), people in any other marital status (about 91%), people listed as unmarried (about 81%), people not in a family (about 75%) and women (about 84%).

Compared with a professional specialty in the private sector, other service (about 94%), farming or fishing (about 90%), handlers or cleaners (about 85%), a missing work class (about 79%), machine operators or inspectors (about 78%), self-employment without incorporation (about 77%), the occupations the model does not tell apart (about 73%) and sales (about 68%) clearly raise it, and federal government work (about 48%), protective service (about 52%), executive or managerial jobs (about 54%) and technical support (about 58%) clearly lower it.

Compared with a high-school education, preschool (above 99%) and an academic associate degree (about 72%) raise it, and a 5th-6th grade (about 38%), 10th grade (about 56%) or 7th-8th grade education (about 57%) lowers it (on the training data only).

On the training data only, being born in Colombia (above 99%), Iran (about 88%), Vietnam (about 86%), Thailand (about 84%), China or the Dominican Republic (about 82%), Puerto Rico or Ecuador (about 74%) raises it, being born in the Philippines (about 26%), Yugoslavia (about 27%), Italy (about 45%), England (about 52%), Cuba or Canada (about 56%) lowers it, being Black or American Indian or Eskimo rather than White raises it to about 69%, and a higher census sampling weight lowers it from about 65% to about 60%.

Being born in Honduras lowers it to about 3% (14 people) and being born in Laos raises it to about 98% (17 people), on the training data only, while never having worked (above 99%, 9 people) and unpaid work (about 77%, 17 people) raise it; the model has little data on this.

ann_113.original: Linear backbone (47 standardized inputs, direct edges only; logit of P(income<=50K)). Hypothesis: a sparse logistic-regression term. Evidence: closed form is exactly linear, y=sum w_i x_i (no bias; bias sits at the output). Largest regular effects (logit, 1 vs 0 or per SD): Wife -4.53, Husband -2.56, Not-in-family -2.02, Married-civ-spouse -1.79, education-num -1.09/SD (-0.43 per year), male -1.10, age -0.585/SD (-0.043/yr), Exec-managerial -0.84, Prof-specialty -0.47, Tech-support -0.69, capital-loss -0.31/SD, Farming-fishing +1.14, Handlers-cleaners +0.73, Self-emp-not-inc +0.68, unknown workclass +0.82. Rare categories act as switches because standardized one-hots are large when 1: Never-worked +20.4 (9 rows), Columbia +8.0 (64), Laos +3.2 (17), Philippines -1.6, Yugoslavia -1.5, Vietnam +1.3. Train mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.799, AUC 0.907->0.714 (the dominant part of the model). Sensitivity (get_viz_summary) equals |w_i|, consistent with linearity. Supported.
ann_113.proposed: The main linear part: a higher education level, older age, capital losses, being a wife and federal, executive or technical jobs lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; not being married, being someone's own child or another relative, being a woman and farming, manual or sales jobs raise it.

ann_114.original: Capital-gain term (entries capital-gain, workclass:4 Private). Closed form: -3.38 cg - 0.95 relu(0.98 cg - 0.0081 wc4 + 0.977 relu(0.687 cg - 0.334) - 0.437) (standardized). Hypothesis (supported): a monotone decreasing, piecewise-linear, concave function of capital gain that lowers P(<=50K); slope -3.38/SD (-0.00045/USD) below ~4.4k USD, -4.31/SD between kinks at ~4.4k and ~4.7k USD (z=0.446, 0.486), -4.95/SD above. Values on train: cg=0 (91.6% of rows) +0.49; 3k -0.89; 5k -1.89; 7k -3.33; 15k -8.4; 99,999 -64.5 (P(<=50K)~0). Workclass Private weight -0.0081 is negligible (sensitivity 4e-4; identical contribution for Private vs not at cg=0). Line plot correlation with cg -0.999. Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.829, AUC 0.907->0.890; the most important nonlinear leaf.
ann_114.proposed: More capital gains lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; work outside the private sector changes it only slightly.

ann_115.original: Hours-per-week term with a Thailand switch (entries hours-per-week, native-country:37 Thailand). Serial ReLU chain 4445->5856->10780->11637 plus direct hours and Thailand edges. Hypothesis (supported): a monotone decreasing, convex piecewise-linear function of hours that raises P(<=50K) for short hours: 4445 is active below ~50 h/week, 10780 below ~19 h; 5856 is always on (bias 1.37) so it is linear in 4445. Contribution on train (non-Thai): 1h +3.45, 10h +2.83, 20h +2.18, 30h +1.59, 40h +0.99, 50h +0.39, 60h +0.23, 80h -0.11, 99h -0.44; slope ~-0.06 logit/h up to 50 h, ~-0.017/h above. Thailand (26 rows) adds a direct +1.15 offset and its -1.55 weight shuts unit 11637, which only matters below ~19 h, so the 'interaction' is practically inert. Sensitivity hours 0.64 vs Thailand 0.076; line plot corr -0.96. Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.849, AUC 0.907->0.902.
ann_115.proposed: Longer working hours lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; being born in Thailand raises it.

ann_116.original: Preschool switch (entries education:13 Preschool, occupation:11 Protective-serv). Chain 6874->6544->1988->12047 plus direct Protective-serv edge. Hypothesis (supported): Preschool is a saturating override, Protective-serv a plain offset; there is no real interaction on data. Train values (3 distinct): neither +0.465; Protective-serv -0.463 (777 rows); Preschool +43.1 (64 rows, P(<=50K)=1 regardless of the rest); no Preschool+Protective-serv rows. The large value comes from the standardized one-hot (~+25 when 1) passing through two stacked positive ReLUs. Sensitivity education:13 0.96, occupation:11 0.13. Mean-ablation changes acc by +0.0008 and AUC by +0.0001 (the override only moves 64 already-confident rows).
ann_116.proposed: A preschool education raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less to above 99%; protective service work lowers it.

ann_117.original: Bachelors offset (education:9). Closed form 0.0816 x + 0.0276 relu(-0.697 x - 0.199): ReLU is on only for non-Bachelors (z=-0.44), off for Bachelors, so the leaf is an exact two-valued offset: Bachelors +0.184, others -0.033 (difference +0.22 logit, i.e. slightly higher P(<=50K) than the education-num term alone predicts). Line plot correlation 1.0. Mean-ablation negligible (acc -0.0004, AUC ~0). Supported.
ann_117.proposed: A bachelor's degree slightly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less through this part.

ann_118.original: Other-service / Without-pay / Iran offsets (entries workclass:8, occupation:8, native-country:20). Closed form 0.539 occ8 - 0.0559 wc8 + 0.262 relu(0.211 Iran + 0.069 occ8 + 0.275 wc8 - 0.288). Hypothesis (supported): additive offsets raising P(<=50K), joined by one ReLU that is off for the reference group (bias -0.288) and on when any of the three is 1, so it is OR-like with near-additive behaviour on data. Train values: none -0.18; Iran +1.28 (45 rows); Other-service +1.62 (3909); Other-service+Iran +3.14 (5); Without-pay +0.51 (15); Without-pay+Other-service +2.36 (2). Sensitivity is dominated by Other-service (0.54). Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.851, AUC 0.907->0.906.
ann_118.proposed: Other service jobs, being born in Iran and unpaid work raise the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less.

ann_119.original: Unmarried offset (relationship:4). relu(1.13 x + 0.82) is always on (linear on data), times output weight -0.451: Unmarried -1.86 vs others -0.20, a -1.67 logit offset. Read together with the backbone's relationship terms (Husband -2.56, Not-in-family -2.02, Wife -4.53), the reference categories Own-child and Other-relative have the highest P(<=50K). Line plot correlation 1.0. Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.848, AUC 0.907->0.906. Supported.
ann_119.proposed: Being listed in the household as unmarried lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less through this part.

ann_120.original: Honduras offset (native-country:16). relu(0.992 x + 0.156) is always on; times -0.076 gives Honduras -3.99 vs others -0.01 (14 train rows). A large offset fitted to very few rows (standardized one-hot ~52 when 1), lowering P(<=50K); likely overfit, no effect on aggregate metrics (ablation changes nothing).
ann_120.proposed: Being born in Honduras lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from only 14 people.

ann_121.original: Never-married offset (marital-status:4). relu(0.598 relu(0.926 x + 0.29) + 0.0113): the inner ReLU is off for non-Never-married rows (z=-0.70) and on for Never-married (z=1.42), so the leaf is an exact two-valued switch; times output weight +0.329: Never-married +0.32 vs others +0.004, a +0.32 logit offset raising P(<=50K) on top of the backbone Married-civ-spouse -1.79. Line plot correlation 1.0 (two values); mean-ablation small (AUC -0.0003). Supported.
ann_121.proposed: Being never married raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less through this part.

ann_122.original: Prof-school offset (education:14). relu(x + 0.023) is ~0 for non-Prof-school (z=-0.13) and 7.7 for Prof-school; times -0.024: Prof-school -0.185 logit (652 rows), others 0. A small offset lowering P(<=50K) beyond education-num. Mean-ablation negligible. Supported.
ann_122.proposed: A professional school degree slightly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less.

ann_123.original: Root composition. P(income<=50K) = sigmoid(1.382 + linear_backbone + capital_gain_hinge + hours_chain_thailand + preschool_protective_gate + bachelors_offset + withoutpay_otherservice_iran - 0.451 unmarried_unit - 0.076 honduras_unit + 0.329 never_married_unit - 0.024 prof_school_unit). Hypothesis (supported): purely additive composition in logit space of one sparse linear backbone and nine independent univariate or small-group terms; no child feeds another, so there are no cross-child interactions. The 46 unconnected inputs are zero-effect entries (no edges; SHAP <= 9.4e-4 = noise). Evidence: closed form via get_formula; train acc 0.851, AUC 0.907; whole-model SHAP (train, 200 samples) ranks Husband, Married-civ-spouse, education-num, Not-in-family, capital-gain, hours, age, Wife, sex. Mean-ablation on train: backbone AUC 0.907->0.714, capital gain ->0.890, hours ->0.902, Other-service group ->0.906, Unmarried ->0.906, others negligible. Function preservation vs original phenotype ~7e-16.
ann_123.proposed: Capital gains and losses, a higher education level, longer hours, older age and being a wife lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; not being married, being someone's own child or another relative, being a woman, and service, farming or manual jobs raise it.

summary.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional specialty job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week with no capital gains or losses), capital gains of $6,849 rather than none clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 63% to about 5%, and moving from 7 to 13 on the 1-16 education scale clearly lowers it from about 86% to about 32%.

Compared with a husband married to a civilian spouse, the model clearly gives a wife a much lower chance (about 19%), and someone's own child or another relative (about 96%), never-married people (about 93%) and people in any other marital status (about 91%) a much higher one.

Working 55 rather than 24 hours a week clearly lowers it from about 82% to about 46%, being 58 rather than 22 years old from about 76% to about 41%, and capital losses of $1,887 to about 28%, while being a woman clearly raises it to about 84%.
Compared with a professional specialty, other service jobs (about 94%), farming or fishing (about 90%) and handlers or cleaners (about 85%) clearly raise it.
A preschool education (64 people) raises it to above 99%, and being born in the Philippines (235 people) lowers it to about 26% (on the training data only).

Largest regular effects (logit, 1 vs 0 or per SD): Wife -4.53, Husband -2.56, Not-in-family -2.02, Married-civ-spouse -1.79, education-num -1.09/SD (-0.43 per year), male -1.10, age -0.585/SD (-0.043/yr), Exec-managerial -0.84, Prof-specialty -0.47, Tech-support -0.69, capital-loss -0.31/SD, Farming-fishing +1.14, Handlers-cleaners +0.73, Self-emp-not-inc +0.68, unknown workclass +0.82. Rare categories act as switches because standardized one-hots are large when 1: Never-worked +20.4 (9 rows), Columbia +8.0 (64), Laos +3.2 (17), Philippines -1.6, Yugoslavia -1.5, Vietnam +1.3. Train mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.799, AUC 0.907->0.714 (the dominant part of the model). Sensitivity (get_viz_summary) equals |w_i|, consistent with linearity. Supported.

parts.name: preschool_protective_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Preschool switch (entries education:13 Preschool, occupation:11 Protective-serv). Chain 6874->6544->1988->12047 plus direct Protective-serv edge. Hypothesis (supported): Preschool is a saturating override, Protective-serv a plain offset; there is no real interaction on data. Train values (3 distinct): neither +0.465; Protective-serv -0.463 (777 rows); Preschool +43.1 (64 rows, P(<=50K)=1 regardless of the rest); no Preschool+Protective-serv rows. The large value comes from the standardized one-hot (~+25 when 1) passing through two stacked positive ReLUs. Sensitivity education:13 0.96, occupation:11 0.13. Mean-ablation changes acc by +0.0008 and AUC by +0.0001 (the override only moves 64 already-confident rows).

parts.name: hours_chain_thailand
parts.original_hypothesis: Hours-per-week term with a Thailand switch (entries hours-per-week, native-country:37 Thailand). Serial ReLU chain 4445->5856->10780->11637 plus direct hours and Thailand edges. Hypothesis (supported): a monotone decreasing, convex piecewise-linear function of hours that raises P(<=50K) for short hours: 4445 is active below ~50 h/week, 10780 below ~19 h; 5856 is always on (bias 1.37) so it is linear in 4445. Contribution on train (non-Thai): 1h +3.45, 10h +2.83, 20h +2.18, 30h +1.59, 40h +0.99, 50h +0.39, 60h +0.23, 80h -0.11, 99h -0.44; slope ~-0.06 logit/h up to 50 h, ~-0.017/h above. Thailand (26 rows) adds a direct +1.15 offset and its -1.55 weight shuts unit 11637, which only matters below ~19 h, so the 'interaction' is practically inert. Sensitivity hours 0.64 vs Thailand 0.076; line plot corr -0.96. Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.849, AUC 0.907->0.902.

parts.name: withoutpay_otherservice_iran
parts.original_hypothesis: Other-service / Without-pay / Iran offsets (entries workclass:8, occupation:8, native-country:20). Closed form 0.539 occ8 - 0.0559 wc8 + 0.262 relu(0.211 Iran + 0.069 occ8 + 0.275 wc8 - 0.288). Hypothesis (supported): additive offsets raising P(<=50K), joined by one ReLU that is off for the reference group (bias -0.288) and on when any of the three is 1, so it is OR-like with near-additive behaviour on data. Train values: none -0.18; Iran +1.28 (45 rows); Other-service +1.62 (3909); Other-service+Iran +3.14 (5); Without-pay +0.51 (15); Without-pay+Other-service +2.36 (2). Sensitivity is dominated by Other-service (0.54). Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.851, AUC 0.907->0.906.

parts.name: unmarried_offset
parts.original_hypothesis: Unmarried offset (relationship:4). relu(1.13 x + 0.82) is always on (linear on data), times output weight -0.451: Unmarried -1.86 vs others -0.20, a -1.67 logit offset. Read together with the backbone's relationship terms (Husband -2.56, Not-in-family -2.02, Wife -4.53), the reference categories Own-child and Other-relative have the highest P(<=50K). Line plot correlation 1.0. Mean-ablation: acc 0.851->0.848, AUC 0.907->0.906. Supported.

parts.name: never_married_offset
parts.original_hypothesis: Never-married offset (marital-status:4). relu(0.598 relu(0.926 x + 0.29) + 0.0113): the inner ReLU is off for non-Never-married rows (z=-0.70) and on for Never-married (z=1.42), so the leaf is an exact two-valued switch; times output weight +0.329: Never-married +0.32 vs others +0.004, a +0.32 logit offset raising P(<=50K) on top of the backbone Married-civ-spouse -1.79. Line plot correlation 1.0 (two values); mean-ablation small (AUC -0.0003). Supported.

parts.name: bachelors_offset
parts.original_hypothesis: Bachelors offset (education:9). Closed form 0.0816 x + 0.0276 relu(-0.697 x - 0.199): ReLU is on only for non-Bachelors (z=-0.44), off for Bachelors, so the leaf is an exact two-valued offset: Bachelors +0.184, others -0.033 (difference +0.22 logit, i.e. slightly higher P(<=50K) than the education-num term alone predicts). Line plot correlation 1.0. Mean-ablation negligible (acc -0.0004, AUC ~0). Supported.

parts.name: honduras_offset
parts.original_hypothesis: Honduras offset (native-country:16). relu(0.992 x + 0.156) is always on; times -0.076 gives Honduras -3.99 vs others -0.01 (14 train rows). A large offset fitted to very few rows (standardized one-hot ~52 when 1), lowering P(<=50K); likely overfit, no effect on aggregate metrics (ablation changes nothing).

parts.name: prof_school_offset
parts.original_hypothesis: Prof-school offset (education:14). relu(x + 0.023) is ~0 for non-Prof-school (z=-0.13) and 7.7 for Prof-school; times -0.024: Prof-school -0.185 logit (652 rows), others 0. A small offset lowering P(<=50K) beyond education-num. Mean-ablation negligible. Supported.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
